title: Pronounced Spatiotemporal Differences of Compound Flooding Inundation in China's Coastal Cities Under Climate Change
content:
Abstract

China's coastal cities face increasingly severe compound flooding driven by rainfall and sea levels under climate change. However, the spatiotemporal variation patterns of compound inundation across China's coast remain insufficiently assessed. Here, we develop a statistical–hydrodynamic coupling framework to quantify historical (1979–2008) and future (2031–2060) compound inundation across 16 major coastal cities under historical, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. We pair design daily rainfall and design peak sea levels for each scenario and six return periods, convert them into 24 hr boundary forcing time series, and drive SFINCS to simulate compound inundation under combined, rainfall-only, and sea level-only conditions. We evaluate inundated area, mean and extreme inundation depth, and quantify dominance drivers and the compound effects. Results reveal strong spatiotemporal differences: the central coast tends to exhibit larger inundation extents, the southern coast deeper mean inundation depths, and the northern coast higher extreme inundation depths. Rainfall exerts stronger control on inundation extent, whereas sea level forcing governs inundation depth, with stronger rainfall dominance for inundated area in northern coast and stronger sea level dominance for mean depth in central coast. Compound effects can significantly increase extreme inundation depth, and their impact on inundated area is most pronounced in the central coast. The extreme inundation depth in Taizhou rises by 1.99 m, while 60% of Shanghai's inundated area will be affected under T = 100 years. This study provides a scientific basis for zonal prevention and control as well as differentiated adaptation strategies addressing compound flooding risk in coastal Chinese cities under climate change.
